blogs.title: Building Investor-Ready Financials for Nigerian Growth Companies
blogs.excerpt: A practical guide for founders and finance teams who want financial statements, controls, and reporting habits that can withstand investor, lender, and board scrutiny.
blogs.content:
## The finance function is now a growth engine

For a growing Nigerian business, finance is no longer just a record-keeping function. Investors, lenders, regulators, and strategic partners want evidence that the company understands its numbers, can explain its performance, and can repeat its results without depending on one founder's memory.

Investor-ready financials are not built the week a term sheet arrives. They are built through consistent monthly discipline: clean books, documented assumptions, reconciled balances, tax clarity, and a management team that can connect financial performance to operating decisions.

## What investors look for first

Before an investor studies valuation, they usually test credibility. They want to know whether the company's financial story is complete, internally consistent, and supported by records.

The first review usually focuses on:

- Revenue quality: who pays, when they pay, how revenue is recognized, and whether it can be traced to contracts or invoices
- Gross margin: whether direct costs are fully captured and allocated correctly
- Cash conversion: how quickly sales become cash and how much working capital the business consumes
- Tax exposure: whether VAT, WHT, PAYE, pension, and company income tax obligations are current
- Controls: who approves spending, who handles cash, and how exceptions are detected

A company does not need to be perfect. It does need to be transparent, consistent, and able to explain its numbers without panic.

## The monthly close discipline

The strongest finance teams treat month-end close as a management ritual, not an accounting chore. Within a defined number of days after month end, the team should produce a concise pack covering profit and loss, balance sheet, cash flow, aged receivables, aged payables, payroll, tax obligations, and key performance indicators.

This habit changes how leadership behaves. Decisions become faster because the team is not debating whose spreadsheet is correct. Forecasts improve because actual results are available early enough to matter. External reviews become less disruptive because the evidence already exists.

## Controls that scale without slowing the business

Many growing companies delay controls because they fear bureaucracy. That is a mistake. Good controls reduce friction when they are designed around real workflows.

A practical control environment includes clear approval limits, segregation of duties, bank reconciliations, inventory checks where relevant, vendor onboarding procedures, expense documentation, and a simple fixed asset register. These controls should be visible enough to guide behavior and light enough that people will actually use them.

The goal is not to make every transaction difficult. The goal is to make unusual transactions visible.

## Preparing for diligence before diligence begins

A business that expects funding, debt, acquisition interest, or major partnerships should maintain a live diligence folder. It should include incorporation documents, tax filings, audited financial statements, management accounts, bank statements, customer contracts, supplier agreements, payroll records, board minutes, insurance documents, and major licenses.

When these documents are kept current, diligence becomes a structured review instead of an emergency. That difference can affect valuation, negotiation leverage, and investor confidence.

## How BYC helps

Babatunde Yunus & Co. helps growth companies move from reactive bookkeeping to decision-grade reporting. We support financial statement preparation, internal control reviews, tax compliance, audit readiness, and management reporting structures designed for Nigerian operating realities.

> The best time to become investor-ready is before capital is needed. The second-best time is before the next month closes.

blogs.title: The Tax Compliance Playbook Nigerian SMEs Should Use Before Year-End
blogs.excerpt: A clear operating playbook for SMEs that want to reduce tax surprises, avoid penalties, and keep leadership focused on growth instead of regulatory firefighting.
blogs.content:
## Compliance is easier when it is designed into operations

Tax problems rarely begin at filing time. They begin months earlier, when invoices are issued without the right treatment, withholding tax credits are not collected, payroll records are incomplete, or VAT is treated as spare cash instead of a liability.

For Nigerian SMEs, the practical answer is not a last-minute scramble. It is a simple compliance rhythm that finance, operations, and leadership understand.

## Build a tax calendar that people actually use

A tax calendar should be visible, owned, and reviewed every month. It should cover VAT, withholding tax, PAYE, pension remittances, annual returns, company income tax, education tax where applicable, and any sector-specific obligations.

The calendar should not sit in a forgotten folder. It should assign responsibility, due dates, evidence required, and escalation rules. If a filing depends on another team, that dependency should be clear before the deadline arrives.

## Reconcile tax positions monthly

Every month, the finance team should reconcile output VAT, input VAT, withholding tax receivables, withholding tax payable, PAYE, and statutory deductions. This allows leadership to know what is owed, what can be recovered, and which documents are missing.

Monthly reconciliation also helps prevent a common SME problem: profitable months that still create cash pressure because tax liabilities were not planned for.

## Keep evidence, not just summaries

Regulators and auditors do not rely on summaries alone. Businesses need invoices, receipts, bank evidence, contracts, payroll schedules, remittance receipts, credit notes, and withholding tax credit notes.

The standard should be simple: if a number is reported, the business should be able to produce the document that supports it. Strong evidence protects the business during audits and makes advisory work more precise.

## Review contracts before tax treatment becomes expensive

Many tax exposures are created by contract wording. Service descriptions, payment timing, reimbursement clauses, cross-border arrangements, and responsibility for withholding tax can all affect the final position.

Before signing major customer, vendor, or consultant agreements, finance should review the expected tax treatment. This is especially important for recurring service contracts, foreign vendors, management fees, technology subscriptions, and related-party arrangements.

## Make tax planning lawful and operational

Good tax planning is not aggressive improvisation. It is the disciplined use of lawful deductions, incentives, timing, structure, and documentation. SMEs should review allowable expenses, capital allowances, employee benefits, bad debt treatment, and available incentives early enough to act properly.

Tax planning works best when it is connected to business planning. A new branch, major equipment purchase, export contract, or financing arrangement can all have tax consequences that should be modeled before decisions are final.

## How BYC helps

BYC supports SMEs with compliance calendars, tax reviews, filing support, audit representation, payroll compliance, and year-end planning. Our work is designed to reduce surprises and give business owners a clear view of their obligations before deadlines become emergencies.

> The healthiest tax position is one leadership can explain before the regulator asks.

blogs.title: Audit Readiness Is a Management Advantage, Not an Annual Event
blogs.excerpt: Why modern businesses should treat audit readiness as a year-round control discipline that improves governance, decision-making, and stakeholder trust.
blogs.content:
## Audit readiness starts before the auditor arrives

Many companies treat audit as a seasonal disruption: gather documents, answer urgent requests, and hope the process ends quickly. Stronger businesses take a different view. They use audit readiness as a year-round management discipline.

When records are organized, controls are clear, and reconciliations are current, audit becomes more efficient. More importantly, leadership gains better information for running the company.

## The difference between records and reliable records

A business may have invoices, bank statements, receipts, and ledgers, yet still struggle during audit. Reliability depends on whether those records are complete, consistent, approved, and connected to the right accounting treatment.

Reliable records answer four questions: what happened, who approved it, why it was recorded that way, and where the supporting evidence is stored. If those questions cannot be answered quickly, the business is not audit-ready.

## Internal controls are a leadership system

Controls are often misunderstood as restrictions. In reality, they are a leadership system for protecting assets, reducing error, and making performance visible.

Useful controls include payment approvals, bank reconciliations, inventory counts, revenue cut-off procedures, receivables review, vendor verification, payroll checks, fixed asset tracking, and periodic review of journal entries.

The strongest controls are simple enough to follow and strong enough to expose exceptions.

## Why audit readiness improves decision-making

Audit-ready companies usually make better decisions because their numbers are cleaner. Management can see margin pressure earlier, spot slow-paying customers, identify leakage, and understand cash movement with less guesswork.

This is where audit readiness becomes strategic. It gives the board and management confidence that decisions are based on evidence, not assumptions.

## Common weak points we see

The most common issues include unreconciled bank accounts, incomplete revenue documentation, poor inventory records, unsupported expense claims, stale receivables, weak segregation of duties, and late tax remittances.

These issues are fixable, but they become expensive when ignored until year-end. A quarterly internal review can catch most of them before they become audit findings.

## A practical readiness checklist

Businesses should maintain a monthly close file, reconcile all bank accounts, review receivables and payables aging, document unusual transactions, update fixed asset records, retain tax filing evidence, and keep board or management approvals accessible.

This checklist does not need to be complicated. It needs to be consistent.

## How BYC helps

Babatunde Yunus & Co. provides statutory audit, internal control assessment, financial reporting support, and audit readiness reviews. We help businesses strengthen the systems behind their numbers so the audit process produces confidence, not confusion.

> Audit readiness is not about passing a test. It is about building a company whose numbers can be trusted.

blogs.title: Nigeria's 2026 tax reform: what changed for businesses
blogs.excerpt: Four new laws took effect on 1 January 2026. Here is what changed for companies — rates, exemptions, levies, the new tax authority and filing rules — and what to do about it.
blogs.author: BYC Tax Team
blogs.content:
## Four laws, one new system

On 26 June 2025 the President signed four tax laws: the **Nigeria Tax Act 2025** (NTA), the **Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025** (NTAA), the **Nigeria Revenue Service (Establishment) Act 2025** and the **Joint Revenue Board (Establishment) Act 2025**. Most of their provisions took effect on 1 January 2026.

The Nigeria Tax Act replaces most of the old tax statutes — including the Companies Income Tax Act, the Personal Income Tax Act and the VAT Act — with a single law. The Tax Administration Act sets one set of rules for registration, filing, assessment and penalties across federal, state and local tax authorities.

For most businesses, the changes fall into six areas.

## 1. FIRS is now the Nigeria Revenue Service

The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) replaced the Federal Inland Revenue Service on 1 January 2026. References to FIRS in older laws and documents are treated as references to the NRS. The Joint Revenue Board replaced the Joint Tax Board.

In practice, you file federal taxes — company income tax, VAT, the development levy and withholding tax on payments to companies — with the NRS. PAYE for most employees still goes to the State Internal Revenue Service where each employee lives.

## 2. Small companies pay no company income tax

A company is a **small company** if its annual turnover is ₦100 million or less, its total fixed assets are not more than ₦250 million, and it does **not** provide professional services. Small companies pay:

- 0% company income tax
- no capital gains tax
- no development levy

The professional services exclusion is the detail most people miss. Law firms, consultancies, accounting practices and similar businesses do not qualify, however small they are.

Small companies still have to file an annual return. Use our [small company checker](/tools/small-company-check) for a first view of where you stand.

## 3. A single 4% development levy

Several separate levies — including tertiary education tax and the IT, NASENI and Police Trust Fund levies — have been replaced by one **development levy of 4% of assessable profits**. It applies to every company except small companies and non-resident companies.

If you budgeted for the old levies separately, rework your tax provision. For many companies the total is similar, but the base and timing differ.

## 4. Company income tax and capital gains

| Item | Before 2026 | From 2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Small company definition | Turnover up to ₦25m | Turnover up to ₦100m and fixed assets up to ₦250m, excluding professional services |
| CIT rate (other companies) | 20% medium, 30% large | 30% |
| Capital gains tax (companies) | 10% | Aligned with the CIT rate |
| Separate levies | Several | One 4% development levy |

There is no longer a separate medium-company rate. A company that was medium-sized under the old rules is either small (0%) or pays the full rate.

Very large companies — those with turnover of ₦50 billion or more, or that belong to a multinational group with global turnover of at least €750 million — must pay at least a **15% minimum effective tax rate**.

## 5. Employees pay tax on new bands

Personal income tax now starts with ₦800,000 a year taxed at 0%, followed by bands of 15%, 18%, 21%, 23% and 25%. The consolidated relief allowance has gone. In its place is a **rent relief** of 20% of annual rent paid, capped at ₦500,000.

Employers have to update payroll to apply the new bands and deductions. We explain the calculation step by step in [PAYE under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025](/blog/paye-under-the-nigeria-tax-act-2025), and you can test figures in our [PAYE calculator](/tools/paye-calculator).

Employees must now also file their own annual return of income from all sources, separately from the return the employer files.

## 6. Stricter administration and higher penalties

The Tax Administration Act raises penalties for late registration, late filing and late payment, and adds interest on unpaid tax. Every taxable person must register and obtain a tax ID. VAT returns remain due by the 21st of the following month, and a nil return is required for months with no sales — unless you are a small business.

> The reforms reward businesses that keep good records. The exemptions depend on figures you can prove, and the penalties fall hardest on those who can't.

## What to do now

1. **Classify your company.** Check turnover, fixed assets and whether your activities count as professional services.
2. **Update your tax provision.** Replace old levies with the 4% development levy and recompute deferred tax at the new rates.
3. **Fix payroll.** Apply the new bands, remove CRA, and collect rent evidence from staff who want rent relief.
4. **Review VAT and WHT processes.** Make sure returns, including nil returns, go to the NRS on time.
5. **Tidy your records.** Turnover and asset figures need to be supported by proper accounts.
6. **Diarise the new dates.** Our [tax calendar](/tools/tax-calendar) lists the monthly and annual deadlines.

If you would like us to review how the reforms affect your business, [get in touch](/contact).

## Sources

- [PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — Nigeria, taxes on corporate income](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/nigeria/corporate/taxes-on-corporate-income)
- [Mondaq — Series on the Tax Reform Acts 2025](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1671386/series-on-the-tax-reform-acts-2025-what-is-new-and-what-you-should-know)
- [Mondaq — How the current tax administration reshapes compliance](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1665224/tax-reform-2025-how-the-current-tax-administration-reshapes-compliance-enforcement-and-business-strategy)
- [Mondaq — The Nigeria Tax Reform Act 2025 and how it affects businesses](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1705160/the-nigeria-tax-reform-act-2025-and-how-it-affects-businesses)
- [Banwo & Ighodalo — Tax Digest, December 2025](https://www.banwo-ighodalo.com/media-files/2025/12/Tax-Digest.pdf)

blogs.title: PAYE under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025: a worked guide for employers
blogs.excerpt: The new tax bands, the end of the consolidated relief allowance, rent relief and the deductions that remain — with a full worked example of a monthly payroll calculation.
blogs.author: BYC Tax Team
blogs.content:
## What changed on 1 January 2026

The Nigeria Tax Act 2025 replaced the Personal Income Tax Act. For payroll, three changes matter most:

- **New tax bands**, starting with ₦800,000 a year at 0% and rising to 25% above ₦50 million.
- **No consolidated relief allowance.** The old CRA — the higher of ₦200,000 or 1% of gross income, plus 20% of gross income — no longer exists.
- **Rent relief.** Employees can deduct 20% of the rent they pay each year, up to ₦500,000.

## Step 1: Start with total income

Total employment income includes basic salary, all allowances (housing, transport, utility, meal and so on), bonuses and taxable benefits in kind. Work on an annual figure, then divide by 12 for the monthly deduction.

## Step 2: Subtract eligible deductions

Section 30 of the Act allows these deductions from total income:

| Deduction | Typical amount |
|---|---|
| Pension (employee contribution) | 8% of basic, housing and transport |
| National Housing Fund | 2.5% of basic salary, if contributing |
| National Health Insurance | Employee contribution, if any |
| Life insurance or deferred annuity premiums | Premiums actually paid |
| Interest on a loan for an owner-occupied home | Interest actually paid |
| Rent relief | 20% of annual rent, capped at ₦500,000 |

Each deduction needs evidence: pension statements, NHF records, insurance receipts, mortgage statements, tenancy agreements and rent receipts. Collect these before you apply the deductions in payroll.

## Step 3: Apply the bands

| Chargeable income | Rate |
|---|---|
| First ₦800,000 | 0% |
| Next ₦2,200,000 | 15% |
| Next ₦9,000,000 | 18% |
| Next ₦13,000,000 | 21% |
| Next ₦25,000,000 | 23% |
| Above ₦50,000,000 | 25% |

## Worked example

Amaka earns ₦500,000 a month — ₦6,000,000 a year. Her basic, housing and transport pay make up all of it. She pays ₦1,200,000 a year in rent, contributes to a pension, and does not contribute to NHF.

1. **Total income:** ₦6,000,000
2. **Pension (8%):** ₦480,000
3. **Rent relief (20% of ₦1,200,000):** ₦240,000
4. **Chargeable income:** ₦6,000,000 − ₦480,000 − ₦240,000 = ₦5,280,000

Now the bands:

- First ₦800,000 at 0% = ₦0
- Next ₦2,200,000 at 15% = ₦330,000
- Remaining ₦2,280,000 at 18% = ₦410,400

**Annual tax: ₦740,400. Monthly PAYE: ₦61,700.** Her effective tax rate on gross pay is about 12.3%.

You can check this — and try other figures — in our [PAYE calculator](/tools/paye-calculator).

## Who is exempt

Employees whose chargeable income is ₦800,000 a year or less pay no tax, and earners on the national minimum wage are exempt. You still record them on payroll and include them in the annual return.

## Remitting and filing

- **Monthly:** remit PAYE to the State Internal Revenue Service of each employee's state of residence. States generally expect payment by the 10th of the following month.
- **Annually:** file the employer's return of all employees' pay and tax by 31 January of the following year.

The Tax Administration Act also requires **employees** to file their own annual return of income from all sources, even when PAYE has been deducted. Let staff know, especially those with rental, business or investment income.

## Common payroll mistakes to avoid

- Leaving CRA in the payroll system after January 2026.
- Granting rent relief without tenancy evidence.
- Calculating pension on gross pay when the contract defines pensionable pay as basic, housing and transport only.
- Paying PAYE to the state where the office is instead of the state where the employee lives.
- Treating one-off bonuses as if they were spread evenly across the year without checking how the state expects them to be taxed.

> If your payroll software was updated by a vendor, test it. Run three or four employees through the calculation by hand and compare.

## Sources

- [PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — Nigeria, individual taxes](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/nigeria/individual)
- [PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — Nigeria, tax administration](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/Nigeria/Individual/Tax-administration)
- [Mondaq — Personal income tax deductions under the Nigeria Tax Act 2025](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1751764/comprehensive-guide-personal-income-tax-deductions-under-the-nigeria-tax-act-2025)
- [Mondaq — Understanding the taxation of income of employees under the tax reform acts](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1702500/understanding-the-taxation-of-income-of-employees-under-the-tax-reform-acts)

blogs.title: The small company exemption: who qualifies and what you still have to file
blogs.excerpt: Zero company income tax sounds simple. The three tests, the professional services exclusion, and the filing obligations that remain explain why many businesses get it wrong.
blogs.author: BYC Tax Team
blogs.content:
## The headline

From 1 January 2026, a **small company** in Nigeria pays 0% company income tax, no capital gains tax and no development levy. Before the reform, only companies with turnover up to ₦25 million paid 0%. The threshold is now four times higher, so many more businesses qualify — but not all of the ones that think they do.

## The three tests

A company must meet **all three** at the same time:

1. **Turnover** — annual gross turnover of ₦100 million or less.
2. **Fixed assets** — total fixed assets not more than ₦250 million.
3. **Activity** — the company does not provide professional services.

## The professional services exclusion

This is where most misunderstandings start. A small law firm, audit practice, management consultancy, engineering consultancy or architecture practice does **not** qualify, even if its turnover is ₦20 million. It pays company income tax at the full rate and the 4% development levy.

If your business mixes trading and advisory work, look at what actually generates the income. Where it is mainly fees for expert or professional services, assume you are excluded and take advice.

## Turnover and assets need evidence

The exemption depends on numbers. If the NRS questions your status, you need accounts that show turnover and a fixed asset register that supports the asset figure. Businesses that run largely on cash, or mix personal and business spending, will find this hardest.

## What you still have to do

The exemption removes tax, not obligations. A small company must still:

- **File an annual company income tax return**, six months after its year-end.
- **Deduct and remit PAYE** for employees.
- **Deduct withholding tax** on payments where it applies.
- **Keep proper books and records.**
- **Register for tax** and keep registration details up to date.

Small businesses are also exempt from filing monthly VAT returns under the Tax Administration Act.

## Watch for these traps

- **Growing past ₦100 million.** Plan ahead: once you cross the threshold, the full rate and the levy apply, and monthly VAT filing starts.
- **Asset purchases.** A large equipment or property purchase can take you over ₦250 million even if turnover stays low.
- **Splitting the business.** Creating several companies to keep each one under the limits can be challenged as tax avoidance.
- **Capital gains.** The CGT exemption applies to small companies only; the same disposal in a larger company is taxed.

## A quick example

| | Trading company | Consultancy |
|---|---|---|
| Turnover | ₦90m | ₦45m |
| Fixed assets | ₦20m | ₦8m |
| Professional services? | No | Yes |
| Assessable profit | ₦15m | ₦15m |
| Company income tax | ₦0 | ₦4.5m (30%) |
| Development levy | ₦0 | ₦0.6m (4%) |

Two businesses with the same profit, one paying nothing and the other ₦5.1 million — purely because of what they sell.

Try your own figures in the [small company checker](/tools/small-company-check), or [ask us](/contact) to confirm your status.

## Sources

- [PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — Nigeria, taxes on corporate income](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/nigeria/corporate/taxes-on-corporate-income)
- [Banwo & Ighodalo — Tax Digest, December 2025](https://www.banwo-ighodalo.com/media-files/2025/12/Tax-Digest.pdf)
- [Mondaq — How does the new Tax Act affect SMEs?](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1674276/tax-tuesday-how-does-the-new-tax-act-affect-smes)
- [Mondaq — The Nigeria Tax Reform Act 2025 and how it affects businesses](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1705160/the-nigeria-tax-reform-act-2025-and-how-it-affects-businesses)

blogs.title: Every tax deadline a Nigerian business needs to know in 2026
blogs.excerpt: The monthly and annual dates for PAYE, VAT, withholding tax and company income tax under the new tax laws — and a simple routine to never miss one.
blogs.author: BYC Tax Team
blogs.content:
## Why deadlines matter more in 2026

The Nigeria Tax Administration Act 2025 raised penalties for late filing and late payment and added interest on unpaid tax. Taxes you collect from other people — PAYE from employees and withholding tax from suppliers — attract the heaviest consequences if you don't pass them on.

## Every month

| Date | Obligation | Paid to |
|---|---|---|
| 10th | PAYE deducted from the previous month's salaries | State IRS of each employee's residence |
| 21st | VAT return and payment for the previous month | NRS |
| 21st | Withholding tax deducted in the previous month | NRS (companies) or State IRS (individuals) |

A few points that catch people out:

- **Nil VAT returns.** If you are registered and made no sales, you still file by the 21st. Small businesses are exempt from VAT returns.
- **PAYE timing.** State IRSs generally expect PAYE by the 10th. The Tax Administration Act's penalty provision refers to the 21st, but we advise clients to keep paying by the 10th.
- **WHT credit notes.** Make sure the tax you withhold is remitted under your suppliers' tax IDs so they can claim credit.

## Every year

| Date | Obligation |
|---|---|
| 31 January | Employer's annual PAYE return for the previous year |
| 30 June | Company income tax return for a 31 December year-end |
| 6 months after year-end | Company income tax return for other year-ends |

**New companies** file their first return within 18 months of incorporation or 6 months after their first accounting period ends, whichever comes first.

**Employees** must also file their own annual return of income from all sources under the new law. Check your State IRS for its date.

## Company law deadlines

Separately from tax, companies file **annual returns with the Corporate Affairs Commission** every year. Missing them leads to penalties and can make your company appear inactive to banks and counterparties.

## A routine that works

1. **By the 5th:** close payroll and prepare the PAYE schedule.
2. **By the 10th:** pay PAYE and file the evidence.
3. **By the 15th:** reconcile sales and purchases for VAT and list all withholding tax deducted.
4. **By the 21st:** file VAT and WHT returns and pay.
5. **Every quarter:** check your tax accounts with the NRS and the state for any unexplained balances.

Use our [tax deadline calendar](/tools/tax-calendar) to see what is due this month, or [ask us](/contact) to run the routine for you.

## Sources

- [PwC Worldwide Tax Summaries — Nigeria, tax administration](https://taxsummaries.pwc.com/Nigeria/Individual/Tax-administration)
- [Banwo & Ighodalo — Tax Digest, December 2025](https://www.banwo-ighodalo.com/media-files/2025/12/Tax-Digest.pdf)
- [Mondaq — The tax reforms and your statutory filing obligations](https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/tax-authorities/1691640/know-your-taxes-the-tax-reforms-and-your-statutory-filing-obligations-a-simplified-guide)
